title: Paraguay’s Next Development Chapter
text:
Paraguay’s Next Development Chapter

Photo: NORBERTO DUARTE/AFP via Getty Images

Commentary
by

Juliana Rubio
and
Henry Ziemer

Published September 18, 2026

Once relatively overlooked compared to its neighbors, Paraguay is experiencing a surge of interest from the United States and other international players. The South American country posted an impressive real GDP growth rate of 6.6 percent in 2025, the highest of any country in the region bar Guyana. President Santiago Peña has strengthened relations with the United States, attending the inaugural Shield of the Americas Summit in March and joining the White House in pushing for more aggressive security policies to curtail the influence of organized crime. Paraguay’s position as the sole country in South America that maintains diplomatic recognition of Taiwan is another key element of its strategic status, making the country a bulwark against China’s rising influence in the region. Meanwhile, the country’s abundant green energy supplied by the Itaipu and Yacyretá dams is a strategic advantage and draw for foreign investors.Despite impressive growth, Paraguay is building from a lower baseline than its neighbors and fellow Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR) members, such as Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay. Paraguay continues to face structural limitations tied to factors including infrastructure deficits, informality, and rule of law and governance weaknesses. Infrastructure has not kept up with the pace of Paraguay’s economic growth. The country faces an energy grid with limited capacity, poor transportation connectivity within the country and export routes, and insufficient infrastructure to support greater industrial growth. These issues, coupled with limited human capital, have also made it difficult for Paraguay to climb the rungs of value-added manufacturing, leaving its economy largely dependent on agricultural commodity exports. In terms of rule of law, Paraguay faces persistent challenges related to checks on government power, the effectiveness and independence of the judicial system, and institutional accountability.Despite these challenges, Paraguay has the potential to transform its development story—but it will require close cooperation with international partners to make the best use of its advantages. To assess where this international cooperation has focused, and where it needs to focus in the future, the CSIS Americas Program recently spent a week conducting field research in Paraguay, where researchers led semi-structured interviews with dozens of experts, private sector participants, members of civil society, international development partners, and other diplomatic representatives.Paraguay’s Development LandscapeParaguay has experienced significant economic growth over the past 20 years thanks to its macroeconomic stability, contributing to a strengthened agricultural sector, export expansion, and overall greater investor confidence. The country’s economic and political stability, coupled with recent growth and a sound fiscal environment, is reflected in part by its sovereign credit rating trajectory, generating a positive outlook for attracting more long-term investment.It is notable that GDP growth has been coupled with dramatic poverty reduction, from 50 percent in 2005 to just 16 percent in 2025, below countries such as Brazil, Colombia, and Peru. Paraguay’s success reducing poverty has been possible thanks to the country’s focus on the creation of more and better jobs, rising household incomes, heavy investment in infrastructure, human capital development, and targeted social programs. Sustained growth, however, will depend on how Paraguay addresses key challenges that have remained unresolved in spite of strong economic fundamentals.Economic Diversification and Human Capital: While the agriculture sector has been a key driver for economic growth, overreliance on commodities exposes Paraguay’s economy to external risks, while keeping the country concentrated on lower-value production. Moreover, while large agribusinesses generate significant profit, they do not yield the same number of jobs, contributing to inequality as most workers remain concentrated in low-productivity sectors and informality. This imbalance persists even as employment has grown, since informality keeps the tax base small, while low productivity among small- and medium-sized enterprise (SME) keeps the country concentrated in lower-end productive activities.Human capital gaps in more technical sectors also constrain growth as the country seeks to move to higher-value activities and production. Weak education outcomes and lack of access to quality education at primary and secondary levels are also detrimental to the development of qualified talent, because even if higher-level and technical education become available, the talent pipeline will not generate enough qualified candidates to eventually fill positions in higher-value activities.Infrastructure and Connectivity: The country’s energy abundance is checked by weak grid connectivity, meaning that a large portion of the electricity generated is lost in transmission, while overreliance on hydropower leaves the power sector vulnerable to climate-related disruptions. During an interview, an expert asserted that energy demand is growing by 20 percent annually and that, if this trend continues, demand will surpass reliable capacity by 2030, without counting the demand that would come with further industrial expansion. There are also significant transportation challenges, such as poor road conditions, with only 13 percent of roads paved. When it comes to cross-border connectivity, the Capricorn Bioceanic Corridor, a road that connects the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, is still unfinished at key border points with Brazil and Argentina. These bottlenecks in a landlocked country translate into higher transportation costs that reduce competitiveness in the international market. The country is also heavily reliant on river transport, which itself faces infrastructure challenges, coupled with environmental and weather-related restrictions.Governance, Rule of Law, and Transparency: While Paraguay has remained politically stable in recent decades, the country continues to face ruling-party dominance, clientelism, corruption, limited judicial independence, and uneven transparency. The country’s biggest challenge lies in the implementation and enforcement of its rules and laws. According to Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perception Index, Paraguay is ranked 150 out of 182 countries, putting it below regional peers such as Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, and Guatemala. The removal of opposition senator and anti-corruption champion Senator Kattya González in 2024, with fewer votes than the Senate’s rules require for removal, and the recent Supreme Court ruling to uphold the decision, also highlight the fragility of judicial independence and due process, where legal procedures are treated as flexible tools as opposed to binding rules. For the business sector, the inconsistent application of rules and laws in any context is particularly worrisome, and the investment climate is indeed weakened by this judicial insecurity, as well as by weak contract enforcement, lengthy judicial processes, and complications in resolving disputes with government institutions.Geopolitical Risk: Paraguay’s continued recognition of Taiwan also came to the fore in several interviews. As with Taiwan’s other diplomatic allies in Latin America and the Caribbean, China has been aggressively courting Paraguayan politicians and members of the business community in a bid to flip the country’s diplomatic recognition. While the current Peña administration has demonstrated firm commitment to maintaining recognition of Taiwan, several interviewees emphasized impending elections in 2028 as a natural moment where the country’s diplomatic arrangements will come up for debate. Portions of the country’s agricultural sector remains staunch advocates for recognition of China, in hopes that doing so may open new economic opportunities, particularly for beef exports. The agricultural sector is also a powerful lobby within Paraguay.Other interviewees critiqued the United States’ approach of encouraging Paraguay to maintain its recognition of Taiwan without offering favorable access to U.S. markets to offset the cost of shutting China out. These dynamics have a marked impact on Paraguay’s development landscape. While the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund (TaiwanICDF) is a key development partner for the country for now, Taiwan is wary of committing significant resources only for Paraguay to drop its recognition in the next electoral cycle. This has accordingly conditioned Taiwan’s development strategy in Paraguay, which has focused on building durable ties through technical assistance programs, human capital development efforts, and educational exchanges. Priorities for International CooperationParaguay’s development partners have made impressive strides in sectors such as health, agriculture, and human capital development. Building on these, further support to help Paraguay move to its next chapter of development could focus on helping its agriculture move higher up the value chain, strengthening human capital, and further developing an entrepreneurial ecosystem and more formal and productive SMEs. Continued support for health will also be key to advancing general development and worker productivity, while also strengthening a system that can improve efficiency and transparency within government services. Physical infrastructure projects, including road and rail connectivity efforts and grid modernization, also suffer from a lack of interest within the broader development community. Gaps also remain with respect to governance and transparency initiatives, especially following the Trump administration’s severe cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).AgricultureDevelopment partners are active in this sector. For instance, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Office (FAO) 2025 Investment Proposal seeks to strengthen aquaculture quality, freshness, and safety from tank to table, while also developing local market strategies and diversification. For its part, TaiwanICDF has supported the commercial production of surubí, which is widely consumed by the local population, as well as other projects producing tilapia, now integrated as a basic meal into the national school-feeding program, and developing pacú fry, as the species faces significant conservation pressures. These aquaculture projects have developed local technical capacities for fish breeding and production, expanded access to affordable fish for local consumption, and diversified commercially viable species. Combined with the work of organizations including the German Society for International Cooperation and FAO—which, according to interviewees, have focused more on subsistence agriculture than on agriculture as a business—Taiwan could complement these efforts placing greater emphasis on increasing production volumes and developing areas such as traceability that could help producers access new markets, as well as directly connecting producers to markets.Building on past floriculture projects focused on strengthening flower production, farmer training, infrastructure, and market access, TaiwanICDF’s current orchid work represents an evolution toward a more specialized industry, adding the use of technical skills and technology, such as tissue culture techniques and tools to improve commercial production and market access.Broadly, TaiwanICDF can continue providing producers with practical and specialized techniques, focusing on creating stronger links between producers and consumers by using marketing strategies, supporting exhibitions, organizing production groups, and introducing new commercially viable products.Human Capital Development and SMEsDevelopment partners with more specialized technical expertise may be particularly well suited to supporting higher-level technical training in areas tied to Paraguay’s future economic opportunities. For instance, burgeoning interest in the country as a destination for AI data centers has driven speculation about spillover effects for Paraguay’s digital economy and opportunities for server or semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging. However, Paraguay needs more skilled workers to take advantage of these opportunities. An example of a targeted approach is the Polytechnic University Taiwan–Paraguay, founded in 2018 with the objective of training the next generation of engineers as Paraguay seeks to develop the skilled labor needed to move higher up the value chain in sectors ranging from agriculture to information and communication technologies. Now, the government and development partners focused on basic education need to build a stronger pipeline for students, while private national and international actors can further support this initiative by connecting students directly to jobs.Entrepreneurship and SME development will also be important to translate Paraguay’s growth into more formal and productive employment. The goal should be to help informal businesses formalize and support those with potential to grow beyond small-scale activities. Interviews pointed to the importance of moving initiatives beyond pilot programs and better connecting SMEs to financing, technology, markets, and export opportunities. A 2026 investment matchmaking initiative between the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and REDIEX, Paraguay’s investment agency, provides one example of how development cooperation can connect Paraguayan projects directly with international capital. Taiwan’s support could focus on gaps where its practical technical expertise can help SMEs improve productivity, digitalize, meet market standards, become more investment-ready, or connect with Taiwanese companies and markets.HealthAccess to quality, affordable healthcare in Paraguay is uneven, with rural and indigenous communities facing more limited access to hospitals than urban populations. In the development space, both TaiwanICDF and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) have been involved in projects seeking to expand and streamline access to healthcare. KOICA has worked on physical hospital infrastructure for well over a decade, and in 2025 it announced the establishment of a new dental hospital. TaiwanICDF, meanwhile, has emphasized the digital aspect with its Health Information System (HIS) project. In cooperation with Paraguay’s Ministry of Information and Communication Technologies, the HIS provides a unified digital platform that allows hospitals and administrators to view wait times, bed availability, medication orders, and a host of other data points across the public health system. While the HIS project began in 2016, adoption has surged under the Peña administration, and the program now counts more than 1,200 hospitals enrolled according to data shared with the CSIS researchers. HIS also serves a valuable transparency and anticorruption function, making it easier to monitor anomalous behavior such as money laundering via prescription drug orders.

GovernanceHistorically, USAID supported democracy and governance programs focused on transparency, anti-corruption, and institutional strengthening. Whereas other development agencies such as TaiwanICDF and KOICA tend to coordinate directly with the Paraguayan government, USAID partnered with civil society organizations based in Paraguay that were able to serve as watchdogs. The disruption and reduction of USAID’s role in foreign assistance creates a gap in an area where the United States had traditionally been active and could open an opportunity for democratic partners like Taiwan to step up.At the multilateral level, the IDB has supported Paraguay’s transparency agenda and, together with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), has worked on identifying legal and institutional gaps in public governance. OECD reporting also shows the gap between Paraguay’s formal rules and actual implementation, especially on political finance and transparency of public information. Investing in governance and anti-corruption efforts can pay geopolitical dividends as well, helping Paraguay better identify untoward influence campaigns orchestrated by China. Digitalization of government functions could be one area where Taiwan might be able to leverage lessons from its previous partnership with Paraguay on the HIS in broader government procurement or the judicial system. Finally, Taiwan could also expand engagement with civil society and related actors to ensure projects are visible beyond the governmental sphere.InfrastructureParaguay must act quickly to modernize its energy infrastructure and build out additional capacity in other energy sources such as solar, wind, and potentially nuclear. As Taiwan and the United States advance their data center projects with Paraguay, the two countries should also set aside a portion of their investments to help with grid modernization initiatives and on-site energy generation projects to help offset growing energy usage. With respect to transportation, the IDB has been supporting the Bioceanic Corridor, but the project faces obstacles, including the fact that, while the route could bring new opportunities to the country’s historically neglected Chaco region, it may also run afoul of local communities and environmental protections.Conclusion: Paraguay’s MomentA confluence of factors is contributing to Paraguay’s growing regional and global importance. This brings new opportunities in the form of foreign investment and development finance but also creates new fault lines for Asunción to navigate. For the United States and Taiwan, helping Paraguay continue its positive trajectory on government transparency and economic development should be a top priority, including through greater cooperation between development players based on their respective strengths to fill some of the gaps.Juliana Rubio is associate director in the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, D.C. Henry Ziemer is a fellow in the CSIS Americas Program.
